spoken: On the 23rd of October 1956, students in Budapest marched with Hungarian flags that had a hole in the middle.
They had cut out the Communist crest. By midnight, their march had become an uprising.
For twelve days, Hungarians fought, ran their own towns and factories, and forced a new government.
The day before, students at the Technical University had drawn up sixteen demands. They wanted Soviet troops out, free elections, and Im-reh Nodge in government.
Their march, in sympathy with Poland's reforms, was banned, and then allowed. At three in the afternoon, it set off from Pest and from Buda.
The two columns met at the statue of General Bem, and there the flag with the hole appeared.
By six in the evening, the crowd before Parliament was at least 200,000, perhaps 300,000 strong, the United Nations committee estimated.
At eight, the party leader, Air-nur Gair-ur, condemned what he called nationalist demonstrations on the radio.
At about nine, Im-reh Nodge spoke briefly from a balcony, and asked the crowd to go home.
At about half past nine, by the City Park, a crowd pulled down the huge Stalin statue.
At the Radio, guarded by the AVH secret police, students wanted their demands broadcast.
Shortly after nine in the evening, tear gas and then shots came from the building, and people in the street were killed.
That the firing began then is documented. Who fired the very first shot, and on whose order, is still disputed.
Soldiers sent to help the AVH joined the crowd, workers brought arms, and before dawn the first Soviet tanks rolled in.
The tanks came from Soviet bases in Hungary itself. There were about 20,000 troops and 600 tanks, a United Nations inquiry found.
In the morning, the radio named Im-reh Nodge prime minister, and announced martial law in his name. He later said he had not signed it.
Against the tanks stood armed groups formed overnight, mostly young workers and students, some barely past childhood.
The biggest held the Corvin Passage, round a cinema in Pest's eighth district, ringed by tall houses.
Across the avenue, soldiers in the Kill-ee-ahn barracks, under Colonel Pahl Mah-lay-tair, took the insurgents' side.
The groups struck at tanks on the wide avenues, then withdrew into side streets where tanks with little infantry could not follow.
In Buda, the group at Say-nah Square was led by Yah-nosh Sah-bo, a truck driver of nearly sixty, known as Uncle Sah-bo.
From Cheh-pell, the factory island in the south, workers came north to help the fighters in the city.
Soviet soldiers had been told to crush counter-revolutionary gangs. People argued with them in the Russian they had learnt at school.
The young paid dearly. Of all who died in the fighting that autumn, more than one in five was under twenty.
On Thursday, the 25th of October, people near the Astoria talked with Soviet tank crews. Some climbed aboard, and together they went to Parliament to see Im-reh Nodge.
Between eleven and noon, the unarmed crowd in Ko-shoot Square was fired on from several directions.
Who fired is still argued over. Historians blame Soviet tanks in the side streets, shooters on the rooftops, or Hungarian border guards.
The number of dead is just as disputed. The regime's White Book said 22, and at least 75 are known by name.
The United Nations report gave estimates of 300 to 800, and some witnesses spoke of a thousand. No one was ever called to account.
That day, the party dropped Air-nur Gair-ur as its leader, and put Yah-nosh Kah-dahr in his place.
The next day at Mo-shon-mod-yah-roh-vahr, near the Austrian border, border guards fired on an unarmed crowd outside their barracks.
The 1956 Institute counts 52 dead, and reports at the time said up to 105. In revenge, the crowd killed several officers.
Outside Budapest, there was little fighting at first. In most places, power passed without a fight to revolutionary councils, chosen at public meetings.
From the 24th of October, factories and mines elected workers' councils, and a general strike spread across the country.
In Jur, on the 30th of October, about 400 delegates formed the Transdanubian National Council, which called for neutrality.
On the 27th of October, Nodge brought two Smallholders, Zol-tahn Til-dee and Bay-lah Ko-vahch, into a new government.
At dawn on the 28th of October, a Soviet attack on the Corvin Passage was beaten back, and that day the government ordered a ceasefire.
On the radio, Nodge refused to call the uprising a counter-revolution. It was, he said, a great national and democratic movement.
The AVH was dissolved on the 29th of October. On the 30th, Nodge announced the end of one-party rule, and free elections were promised.
Soviet tanks began to leave Budapest, and Moscow declared that it respected the sovereignty of its allies.
The same day, armed insurgents besieged the Budapest party headquarters on Republic Square, believing prisoners were held there.
Its defenders were young AVH conscripts, party staff and army officers.
When it fell, the men who came out to negotiate were shot. Then the crowd shot or lynched several of the defenders.
In all, 23 defenders died, by the 1956 Institute's count, and attackers died too. Revolutionary organisations condemned the lynchings.
After the 4th of November, the Kah-dahr regime held up these killings as proof of a counter-revolution.
On the 31st of October, as the tanks left, Nodge told a crowd, we are living in the first days of our sovereignty and independence.
That day in Moscow, in secret, Khrushchev told the Soviet leaders, we should not withdraw our troops from Hungary and Budapest.
Leaving, he said, would look like weakness to the West, just as Britain and France were going to war with Egypt.
A new government loyal to Moscow would be set up, and the army was given three days to prepare.
On the 1st of November, Nodge learned that new Soviet divisions were crossing Hungary's eastern border.
The Soviet ambassador, Yuri Andropov, told him the troops were there to cover the withdrawal.
That evening, Nodge declared Hungary neutral, out of the Warsaw Pact, and asked the United Nations to defend its neutrality.
Later, the radio broadcast Yah-nosh Kah-dahr praising the people's glorious uprising. But Kah-dahr had already gone over to the Soviets.
At Sol-nok, the Warsaw Pact commander, Marshal Ivan Konev, gave the order to attack on the 4th of November.
On the 3rd of November, Nodge formed a coalition of four parties, with Pahl Mah-lay-tair as minister of defence.
At noon, talks on the withdrawal began in Parliament, and that evening they went on at the Soviet base at Tur-kurl.
At about ten that night, K G B officers led by Ivan Serov arrested Mah-lay-tair and his delegation.
In twelve days, Hungarians had ended one-party rule, dissolved the AVH, and run their own towns and factories.
Students and workers, young fighters and old, soldiers and neighbours did it together, and many paid with their lives.
Not every death came in battle. Unarmed crowds were fired on, and men of the AVH were lynched.
On Saturday night, the 3rd of November, Budapest went to sleep hoping for a quiet Sunday.
Before dawn, the Soviet tanks began to move.
